sentences: Credit utilization is the most important driver of default risk, and its effect is strong: default risk increases as the share of the credit limit in use rises, with the steepest rise at high utilization.
The number of past delinquencies is the second most important driver, with a moderate to strong effect; default risk jumps once an applicant has any past delinquency, and it increases with the count.

The two drivers interact strongly: the effect of credit utilization grows with the number of past delinquencies, and the effect of past delinquencies reverses its sign as utilization changes, so a delinquency adds little risk at low utilization but a large amount at high utilization.
Income has a moderate effect and default risk decreases with it, ranking third or fourth; past delinquencies matter more than income.
The length of credit history has at most a moderate effect, with default risk decreasing as history lengthens, and it ranks somewhere between third and eighth.
The debt-to-income ratio has at most a moderate effect, with default risk increasing as it rises, and it ranks fourth to eighth.
The number of recent credit inquiries hardly matters for default risk, accounting for about 1.6% of the model's importance.

Age, months at the current address and the number of dependents have little or no detectable effect on default risk; age and months at address hardly matter, and the number of dependents has at most a moderate effect.
The data do not settle whether credit utilization interacts with the length of credit history or with the number of dependents.
